Buttondown — Newsletter software for people like you

segments: An independent writer or artist moving a small personal newsletter away from a cumbersome general-purpose email platform
A software developer fitting a headless or Markdown newsletter into an existing code-and-Git workflow
A newsletter owner bringing an editor or operations teammate into a formerly solo publishing workflow

business.what_it_does: Buttondown is a browser-based newsletter service for writing, publishing, and managing email newsletters with rich-text or Markdown editing, subscriber management, automations, paid subscriptions, analytics, teams, an API, and a CLI.
business.business_model: Subscription software priced by total subscriber count, with optional monthly paid add-ons and no percentage fee on paid subscriptions or sponsorships.

facts.statement: Buttondown describes itself as the easiest way to start and grow a newsletter.

provenance.quote: Welcome to Buttondown, the easiest way to start and grow your newsletter.

facts.statement: Buttondown runs entirely in the browser and requires no installation.

provenance.quote: Buttondown is entirely based in your browser. There's nothing to install, so registration is quick and easy.

facts.statement: The editor supports both WYSIWYG rich text and Markdown.

provenance.quote: Our editor is best-in-class, allowing you to write WYSIWYG with rich text – and in Markdown, the lightning-fast language that has become standard throughout the industry.

facts.statement: Teams can review drafts, suggest changes, and work under role-specific permissions.

provenance.quote: Invite collaborators to review your emails before they go out. They can see your drafts, suggest changes, and help you ship with confidence.

facts.statement: Buttondown says there is no limit on the number of collaborators invited to a team.

provenance.quote: No. You can invite as many collaborators as you need.

facts.statement: Team members do not count toward subscriber limits or affect billing.

provenance.quote: No. Team members are collaborators, not subscribers. They don't affect your billing at all.

facts.statement: The REST API supports subscriber management, email sending, and automation creation, and is available on all plans, including free.

provenance.quote: Everything you can do in Buttondown, you can do with the API. Manage subscribers, send emails, create automations — all from your own code.

facts.statement: Buttondown does not take fees from publishers' paid subscribers.

provenance.quote: And we don’t take fees from your paid subscribers.

facts.statement: Buttondown says it is GDPR-compliant and collects no data about publishers or subscribers by default.

provenance.quote: Buttondown is GDPR-compliant and then some. We don't collect any data about you or your subscribers by default.

facts.statement: Human support is generally available from 6am to 6pm US Eastern time, excluding weekends and major holidays.

provenance.quote: We're distributed around the world, and generally available from 6am-6pm US Eastern time (excluding weekends, and major holidays).

facts.statement: The Buttondown CLI supports offline Markdown editing, version control, bidirectional content synchronization, media management, and scripted workflows.

provenance.quote:
The CLI provides several capabilities:

- **Work offline** with your newsletter content
- **Edit in your favorite editor** using Markdown
- **Version control** your newsletters with Git or other tools
- **Sync content** bidirectionally between your computer and Buttondown
- **Manage media files** like images and attachments
- **Automate workflows** with scripts

facts.statement: Buttondown is profitable, self-funded, fully remote, and says it has operated since 2017.

provenance.quote: We're a small team of engineers, writers, and designers who are passionate about making emails better, fully remote and have been since our founding in 2017. We're profitable, self-funded, and have no plans to change that.

facts.statement: The feature overview describes unlimited newsletters charged by total subscriber count, while the pricing page separately lists Multiple newsletters as a +$29/month add-on.

provenance.quote: Create as many distinct newsletters as you'd like – you're only charged for your total subscribers.

facts.statement: The Teams feature page says collaborators are unlimited, the documentation places Teams on the Professional plan and requires a paid account, and the pricing page lists Teams as a +$79/month add-on.

provenance.quote: Available on the Professional plan.

facts.statement: Published prices assume at most one email per day to the entire subscriber base; higher sending frequency requires contacting Buttondown about usage-based pricing.

provenance.quote: All of these prices assume that you're sending at most one email a day to your entire subscriber base. If you're sending more than that, you'll need to contact us and we can talk about what usage-based pricing would look like for you.

entries.claim: Buttondown includes a WYSIWYG editor in addition to its Markdown editor.

exemplars: Most newsletters start as a solo effort. But as yours grows, you'll want help — an editor to catch typos, a collaborator to manage subscribers, a teammate to handle the operational side. Buttondown for Teams makes that easy.

Control exactly what each collaborator can see and do. Give your editor access to drafts but not billing. Let your marketing lead manage subscribers without touching your API keys. Everyone gets the tools they need and nothing they don't.

We know that you don't want to talk to a bot, so our small team of real humans is here to help. 💙 We're distributed around the world, and generally available from 6am-6pm US Eastern time (excluding weekends, and major holidays). objections.objection: Switching providers could lose subscribers, archives, settings, or working automations, so staying with the current platform feels safer than migrating.
objections.answer: Buttondown offers free migration regardless of list size and separately promises concierge migration within one business day after the customer creates an account and contacts the company. The evidence does not specify every source platform, migrated object, or technical exclusion, so it reduces but does not eliminate migration risk.

objections.objection: The price after 100 subscribers is unclear, and the paid add-ons could make a seemingly simple newsletter materially more expensive.
objections.answer: The first 100 subscribers cost nothing, and Buttondown says base charges are tied to active subscribers. Published add-ons range from +$9/month to +$79/month. The supplied evidence does not provide base subscriber-tier prices above 100, so the total cost cannot be resolved from this material.

objections.objection: The offer is internally inconsistent about whether multiple newsletters and Teams are included, plan-based, or separately billed add-ons.
objections.answer: The supplied evidence does not reconcile these conflicts: the feature overview says newsletters are unlimited and priced by total subscribers, while pricing lists Multiple newsletters at +$29/month; Teams documentation places Teams on the Professional plan, while pricing lists Teams at +$79/month. A buyer needs clarification from Buttondown before relying on either interpretation.

objections.objection: A team may not justify paying +$79/month merely to review drafts and separate permissions, especially when shared documents already handle review.
objections.answer: Buttondown supports unlimited collaborators without per-seat charges, role-specific permissions, draft review, immediate access revocation, and an audit trail. Those capabilities answer the control and scaling concern, but the evidence provides no ROI comparison that establishes the add-on is worth +$79/month for a small team.

objections.objection: A developer may reject the platform because it has no official SDK and no official MCP server, leaving integration and client maintenance to the customer.
objections.answer: Buttondown maintains an OpenAPI specification, supports generated typed clients through third-party generators, makes the REST API available on every plan including free, and lets users create multiple permissioned API keys. This enables integration but does not replace an officially maintained SDK or MCP server.

objections.objection: The media workflow is too limited for a newsletter centered on podcasts, video, or large downloadable resources.
objections.answer: Buttondown does not natively host audio or video for inline playback. It can embed hosted content from services including SoundCloud, Spotify, Transistor, YouTube, and Vimeo, and larger files can be linked from external storage. Attachments exist, but the supplied documentation conflicts on whether the per-file limit is 1 MiB or 2 MB and separately limits an email to three files.

objections.objection: Human support is unavailable on weekends and major holidays, which may be unacceptable when a scheduled send, deliverability problem, or paid newsletter fails at the wrong time.
objections.answer: No supplied evidence resolves weekend or major-holiday coverage, and Buttondown states no response-time or resolution SLA.

objections.objection: An independent, self-funded provider may feel more exposed to continuity risk than a large incumbent, making a long-term migration hard to approve.
objections.answer: Buttondown says it has operated since 2017, is profitable and self-funded, and intends to remain independent. One customer reported remaining happy nearly three years after choosing it. These are useful trust signals, but they are not a continuity guarantee or audited financial evidence.

objections.objection: A personal publisher may worry that the service will evolve into another growth-marketing suite, social network, or curated feed that gets between the writer and readers.
objections.answer: Customer statements describe Buttondown as focused on essentials and as a newsletter backend rather than a social network or curated feed. Buttondown also identifies itself as a small independent business and says customer feedback drives its roadmap. These signals address product direction but do not contractually guarantee it will never change.
